title: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
desc: Defines varying autonomy levels and orchestration benefits while emphasizing error propagation and contested human intervention points.

kps.k: Agentic legal AI shifts the debate from generating answers to delegating connected work, but the label covers materially different levels of autonomy.
kps.d: The central proposition is that AI can plan tasks, select tools, gather context and execute successive steps instead of leaving lawyers to connect research, drafting and revision manually. Dickason and Fitzpatrick illustrate this through document-production workflows. Definitions remain contested: Shaver and the Legora outlook distinguish adaptive agents from fixed prompt chains, while CoCounsel’s developers include expert-prescribed sequences within a spectrum of agency. Black includes closed-system routing. These differences mean that an agentic product label alone establishes neither adaptive capability nor unattended operation.

qs.q: They build something, they produce a document, they realize that they’ve got to do more research, so they have multiple steps.
qs.a: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason on Agentic Legal AI, Protégé, Shepard’s Verify, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: A workflow itself is hard-coded in some way, whether by system prompts or otherwise on the back end, and there is consistency and no autonomy in the way it is carried out.
qs.a: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Providers locate the proposed advantage in orchestration, specialist tools and persistent matter context—not model intelligence alone.
kps.d: Reed, Weinberg and Fitzpatrick argue for coordinating task-specific capabilities rather than relying on a universal assistant. Dickason describes a surrounding software system that repeatedly supplies new context and lets a model identify missing information. Nay and Madheswaran expect retained client preferences and matter history to reduce repeated instruction and support cumulative improvement. These are architectural arguments and product descriptions, not comparative proof of superior legal outcomes. They also create dependencies on data quality, continuing updates and access to other vendors’ tools; Definely raises database access as an unresolved constraint.

kps.k: The practical opportunity extends beyond drafting to removing handoffs and administrative bottlenecks across legal service delivery.
kps.d: Buckley argues that fragmented information and administration often obstruct work more than drafting or research. Proposed applications connect intake, context gathering, playbook conversion, document review, billing and client collaboration inside existing work environments. Dunlop emphasises avoiding application switching; McIver reports a small note-processing agent that saves time while retaining review. More ambitious accounts from Clio and LegalOn envisage connected matter lifecycles. The distinction matters: a useful embedded assistant or automated step does not by itself establish end-to-end agency.

qs.a: From Athlete to AI: Summize CEO's Legal Tech Entrepreneurial Journey (Tom Dunlop) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Substantive disagreement concerns how much work to delegate and where human intervention must occur, rather than a simple choice between AI and lawyers.
kps.d: CoCounsel’s developers and Harvey’s described productivity suite retain continuing lawyer involvement. Fleisher recommends lighter supervision for internal context gathering and approval before consequential external actions. Lewis rejects unchecked contract review, while Walker reserves market judgment and client-aligned negotiation strategy for experienced lawyers. More expansive proposals permit routine self-service with escalation, including Junestrand’s reported Debevoise portal. The supplied practical guidance requires meaningful supervision of substantive determinations, advice and representative work; it states that autonomy does not change existing ethical duties. These positions leave open how to make oversight effective rather than nominal.

qs.a: How AI Is Reshaping In-House Legal Teams with Nick Fleisher — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Multi-step execution may improve work through tools and feedback, but it can also propagate errors and move the bottleneck into verification.
kps.d: Fitzpatrick proposes model-to-model feedback as a quality-improvement mechanism, and Costigan describes adversarial review before delivery of a first draft. Black counters that fabricated information can feed subsequent steps, compounding mistakes; her warning rests on experimentation and anecdote, not measured error rates. Shaver says verification must examine reasoning and intended meaning, not just citations. Marwaha argues that repeated checking can erase drafting benefits for experienced lawyers, while Buckley says quality control draws on more expensive resources. The resulting economic question is net workflow benefit after checking and correction, not generation speed alone.

qs.q: And then when they take whatever they made up and apply it to something else, which is what would happen in this scenario, it becomes a game of AI telephone.

kps.k: Action-taking requires governance of permissions, identities and downstream connections as well as review of outputs.
kps.d: Shaver recommends renewed vendor security reviews when agent functionality expands and reports firms discovering agent activity without adequate identifiers. She argues that written policies and manual client-prohibition checks cannot sustainably enforce changing requirements. The legal-responsibility discussion paper links broader tool access and reduced intervention to potential harm and diffuse accountability; embedded interfaces may also weaken users’ ability to monitor or override actions. Practical responses include defined roles and prohibitions, client- and matter-specific access controls, traceable actions and review gates. Salesforce’s Slackbot case study adds a concrete self-reported governance model: a permanent human agent manager, risk scoring, expert acceptance testing and regression testing developed over 18 months.

qs.q: Really, law firms should be going back and revisiting security with the provider to ensure that additional questions are asked about how autonomy is handled within the system, what access the agents have to other systems, and so on.
qs.a: Is Legal Tech in a Bubble? — Nikki Shaver · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: For example, even last year, you know, hearing about firms that for example deployed agents and hadn't put in unique identifiers to ensure that they were trackable or traceable within systems and then later kind of looked at some unusual activity thinking who is that who's doing that and suddenly realized  it was an agent.
qs.a: Nikki Shaver — Legaltech Hub (agentic governance and the efficacy turn) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Deployment evidence shows activity and bounded applications, but does not establish broad reliability, savings or readiness for autonomous legal practice.
kps.d: Much of the support consists of vendor roadmaps, demonstrations, practitioner accounts and analogies with software engineering. The Legora launch account reports demonstrated monitoring, relationship mapping and diligence features, not sustained production results. Nadler reports fund documents reaching senior lawyers at an asserted second- or third-year associate standard within hours or less, without independent measurement. In an April 2026 interview, Niles reports some Salesforce tasks running about 100 times faster with higher accuracy, while acknowledging measurement challenges. Such reports differ from forecasts, including Legora’s 2026 trajectory and broader enterprise projections cited by Levine. Shaver’s cautious deployment assessment contrasts with Niles’s urgency to move beyond pilots; neither establishes a universal adoption timetable.

kps.k: Implementation requires workflow redesign, maintained data and human expertise; easier agent creation does not remove those obligations.
kps.d: Reed warns that internal AI remains software requiring construction, monitoring and improvement. Fleisher describes substantial data preparation and client correction of outdated or unwanted material, alongside changes to established work habits. Junestrand reports investing in legal engineering to help customers adopt new workflows. Practitioner accounts from the Everlaw panel and AAA describe process mapping before further construction. A sharper critique in the Tara Waters discussion asks whether faster execution merely reproduces familiar processes. McNairn instead proposes that in-house lawyers build operational infrastructure that embeds legal requirements into procurement and hiring. These approaches differ in ambition but treat purchasing a tool as insufficient.

qs.q: Sometimes people say, "Well, I didn't actually want to include that folder," or, "That playbook is outdated.

qs.q: And there’s a tremendous amount of work and energy and time that needs to go in to how to empower your teams to get the most out of AI.
qs.a: Max Junestrand, Legora: 'We're Setting the Precedent' · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Agentic delivery could change professional roles and client relationships without determining headcount, pricing or provider displacement.
kps.d: Hron predicts a shift from performing work to governing it; Logvinova envisages lawyers supervising multiple digital agents. Nay extends the role to agents checking other agents for legal compliance. These are prospective roles, distinct from Salesforce’s reported agent-manager appointment. Nadler connects automated junior execution to firm economics, but Fleisher rejects like-for-like staffing substitutions and McIver rejects claims that agents necessarily eliminate the billable hour. Niles predicts that credible AI capability will influence outside-counsel selection, while Pereyra and Junestrand see opportunities to package firm expertise into client-facing systems. The evidence leaves pricing, ownership of jointly developed systems and the balance between direct software use and purchased legal services unresolved.

qs.q: Your role now changes from doing the work to governing the work.
qs.a: Legal AI, Trust, and Agents: Joel Hron on Thomson Reuters, Anthropic, and the Future of CoCounsel · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But as the key systems are agentic — so think generating marketing, or talking directly to a client, or giving investment advice as an agent to a client — a lot of stuff that traditionally was human, that core economic activity, needs other AI agents to check that from a legal, regulatory, and compliance perspective.
qs.a: John Nay — Norm Ai / Norm Law (agentic law and the AI-native full-service firm) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: The selected AI-native legal-provider sources accept the proposition that legal AI’s value lies in delegated workflows rather than isolated answer generation, and collectively extend it into concrete service-delivery models. Their common rationale is that AI should perform bounded first-pass or routine execution within redesigned processes, while lawyers retain responsibility at consequential handoffs. Nadler describes integrated agents and skills producing junior-level fund work for senior-attorney review; Berrent develops a direct-to-client, software-first service with embedded legal expertise; and Walker adds persistent context, iterative AI production, licensed-lawyer oversight and prospective integration of legal agents into company processes. Mazares is more cautious and less specifically agentic, emphasizing simple, machine-like tasks, people and effective process. Material variation therefore concerns ambition and locus of delivery: Nadler focuses on automating junior execution, Berrent on client experience and AI-first operations, Walker on context-rich agents embedded in organisational workflows, and Mazares on incremental task automation. None supplies independent comparative evidence establishing broad reliability, net savings after verification or readiness for unattended legal practice; the strongest performance claims remain operational accounts or predictions.

qs.q: Um it's loaded up with the agents and skills that have been built both by the software engineering team and the legal engineering team neatly integrated.

vlens.an: The curated Academia & research sources accept the principal proposition that agentic legal AI moves beyond answer generation toward connected, multi-step action. Their common reasoning is that agency depends on goal-directed execution, tool selection and orchestration, with prospective applications extending from substantive legal work to intake, scheduling, eligibility checks and other administrative workflows. Collectively, they build on the proposition by identifying organisational integration and shared context—not models alone—as foundations for scaled deployment and client trust. Material variation concerns depth and caution: Tellmann offers a technical account of adaptive autonomy while qualifying legal adoption as early-stage; the agentic-law-firm source adds a concrete four-layer organisational architecture and stresses human oversight; Steenhuis gives a simpler action-versus-text framing and prospective legal-aid examples. None provides comparative deployment evidence establishing broad reliability or net savings, and only the agentic-law-firm source directly engages hallucinations, guardrails and human oversight. The sources therefore develop the architecture and application side of the synthesis more than its central concerns about error propagation, verification bottlenecks, permissions and contested intervention points.

qs.q: They set sub-goals, select tools, and  execute multi-step actions in pursuit of defined objectives with minimal supervision.274  Unlike earlier models, they can handle open-ended tasks, adapt dynamically to  unforeseen conditions, and generate novel solutions in natural language.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.
qs.a: How Law Firms Can Lead the Agentic AI Era — And What Clients Now Expect · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: These curated in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the proposition that agentic AI moves legal work from isolated generation toward connected workflow delegation, while requiring workflow redesign and continuing human accountability. They materially extend it from the buyer side by specifying operational governance mechanisms—defined permissions and prohibitions, risk-and-impact scoring, subject-matter-expert acceptance testing, guardrails, regression testing and a permanent human agent-manager role—and by linking credible AI governance to outside-counsel selection and client trust. Common reasons are faster self-service, removal of intake and administrative friction, and preserving lawyers’ time for strategic, relational and judgment-intensive work. Material variation concerns the delegation boundary: Klinger is comparatively expansive, reporting contract self-service and forecasting agents doing work previously assigned to a paralegal or lawyer, whereas the Salesforce sources place stronger emphasis on bounded autonomy, protected context, compliance and human oversight. The operational benefits remain mainly self-reported or forecast, and these sources do not resolve the synthesis’s central economic concern about error propagation and net gains after verification.

The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively accept the proposition that agentic legal AI moves beyond answer generation toward connected, tool-using workflows, and they materially develop it through concrete architectures, deployment patterns and operating models. Common reasons include the value of orchestrating specialist tools and models; grounding systems in persistent matter context, firm knowledge and client-specific playbooks; embedding workflows in existing document, contract, intake and practice-management environments; and retaining human review or escalation for consequential decisions. Several sources further extend the proposition by proposing adversarial model review, agents that govern other agents, lawyer supervision of multiple digital agents, simulated matters for training, and lawyer-led redesign of business operations.

The voice is not uniformly promotional or uniformly expansive. Some sources envisage adaptive end-to-end execution or routine self-service, whereas others limit autonomy to discrete, lower-stakes tasks or expert-prescribed sequences. Human involvement ranges from continuous supervision to confirmation checkpoints or exception-based escalation. A particularly important internal strand directly supports the synthesis’s verification-bottleneck claim: Marwaha argues that repeated checking can erode drafting value, and Buckley says quality control shifts work to more expensive resources. Other vendors claim that tool use, grounding, model feedback or adversarial review will improve reliability, but those claims are generally predictive, illustrative or company-reported rather than independently measured. A few sources redirect attention toward reasoning models, future roles or operational infrastructure, and several are too adjacent to establish a clear position. Overall, however, this professional voice both endorses the core proposition and supplies substantial implementation detail, while leaving broad reliability, net savings after verification and readiness for autonomous legal practice unproven. Because the corpus is curated, this characterises only the supplied vendor sources and does not imply prevalence across legal-tech vendors generally.

vlens.an: This curated set broadly accepts the proposition that agentic legal AI delegates connected, multi-step work and thereby shifts—not removes—the need for human verification and control. It materially develops the proposition in three ways: by specifying governance mechanisms such as renewed security review, unique agent identities, downstream-access controls and client- or matter-level permissions; by describing orchestration layers that coordinate specialised agents; and by arguing that implementation should redesign workflows rather than merely accelerate existing checklists. Material variation concerns the preferred degree of autonomy and the strength of the claims. Some sources favour bounded, structured human–AI workflows and cautious deployment, while others envisage increasingly connected agents or more fundamental process redesign. Press and analyst accounts repeatedly distinguish announcements, forecasts and anecdotal observations from demonstrated reliability or savings; vendor-linked voices are more expansive about orchestration and high-value workflows but still provide architectural or economic rationales rather than comparative performance evidence. None clearly rejects the proposition, although several warn that hype exceeds deployment and that error propagation, verification costs and governance gaps may constrain benefits. Because these sources are curated, this alignment should not be treated as representative of all market analysts, consultancies or press.

vlens.an: This curated set of regulators, courts-associated commentators and professional bodies accepts the synthesis’s principal proposition that agentic AI delegates connected, tool-enabled work across materially different levels of autonomy and shifts the practical problem toward human intervention and verification. It materially develops that proposition by translating it into professional duties and governance questions: autonomy does not displace lawyers’ independent judgment; substantive or representative legal work requires meaningful supervision; and tool permissions, accountability and interface design affect users’ ability to constrain, monitor and override agents. Common reasons include the greater consequences of action-taking compared with answer generation, the risk of relying on processes that run without contemporaneous review, and the need to redesign workflows and controls rather than merely acquire AI tools. Material variation remains. Formal guidance is prescriptive about ethical obligations; the legal-responsibility paper is conceptual and forward-looking about liability and diffuse accountability; Fleisher advocates risk-sensitive checkpoints and doubts near-term end-to-end autonomy; AAA describes practical workflow mapping and hybrid hiring without measured outcomes; and several courts-associated podcast discussions offer more optimistic, conceptual or secondhand accounts while acknowledging unresolved oversight concerns. These sources generally do not provide empirical evidence that agentic systems are broadly reliable, economical after verification, or ready for autonomous legal practice, and the curated selection should not be treated as representative of all institutions or professionals in this voice.

qs.q: Lawyers must not deploy agentic systems in a manner that allows the system to make substantive legal determinations, communicate legal advice, prepare and file pleadings, or otherwise act in a representative capacity without meaningful lawyer supervision 1 and review.

vlens.an: The selected traditional-law-firm voices generally support the proposition’s core claim that AI delegation should be bounded by task complexity, risk and meaningful lawyer verification. Nuara most directly aligns with it: he distinguishes routine, readily checked transaction documents from downstream drafting where mistakes carry greater consequences and quality analysis must be more rigorous. Dhein reaches a similar position through capability matching, arguing that workflows should be decomposed into tasks and that complex legal research remains outside current models’ reliable scope. Together, these accounts reinforce the proposition that connected work should not be delegated wholesale merely because AI can generate or draft quickly. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than opposition: Nuara focuses on transaction risk and review intensity; Dhein focuses on model strengths and task selection; the startup-adoption discussion concentrates on security, compliance and client-data gates. That third source is adjacent but indeterminate on agentic autonomy, error propagation and verification bottlenecks, while its interviewer’s concern about excessive caution remains an unanswered prompt. None of these sources supplies measured evidence on end-to-end agentic reliability or the net economic benefit after verification, so their support is practical and experience-based rather than comparative proof. Because the sources are curated, this assessment characterises only these selected law-firm voices and does not imply prevalence across traditional practice.

qs.q: But then as you go further downstream, you have a higher and higher risk value that you would place on a potential mistake or the misuse of the AI.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition’s core shift from answer generation toward delegation of connected, multi-step work, while treating agenticness as a spectrum rather than a binary product category. Their common reasoning is that greater agency combines goal pursuit, information gathering, tool use and action with less step-by-step supervision; this makes the location and degree of human intervention consequential. Material variation lies in scope and evidential strength: Leonard and McCormack range from describing web retrieval as limited agency to anticipating computer-use systems that pursue overarching goals, but rely substantially on illustrations, forecasts and secondhand reports. The governance paper develops a more systematic, multidimensional account and conditions benefits on reliability, operating costs and safeguards against failures and abuse. Collectively, however, these sources do not establish the cluster’s specifically legal claims about error propagation, verification costs or net workflow savings through measured deployment evidence. Their support is therefore conceptual and qualified, not proof that verification has already become the operative bottleneck in legal practice.

qs.q: Instead, an AI system’s agenticness is best understood as involving multiple dimensions, along each of which we expect the field to continue to progress.
qs.a: Practices for Governing Agentic AI Systems · Legal-tech vendor · 2023

elens.an: Across this curated 2025 set, the sources accept the proposition’s core shift from answer generation to connected, tool-enabled legal workflows and materially develop it with concrete architectures, use cases and operating models. Common reasons include the ability to coordinate specialist tools, retain matter context, remove handoffs and automate bounded steps across intake, research, drafting, contract review, administration and client delivery. They also commonly preserve lawyer control through approval gates, interim review, escalation or hybrid human–AI workflows. Material variation concerns the permitted degree of autonomy: some sources envisage adaptive or end-to-end agents, while others restrict deployment to deterministic, discrete or lower-stakes tasks. Verification receives uneven attention—several sources explicitly warn that repeated checking can erode gains or that current multi-step work is not yet trustworthy, but many vendor accounts discuss oversight only generally and provide roadmaps, demonstrations or unmeasured claims rather than production evidence. Further extensions include lawyers supervising multiple agents, specialist orchestration layers, firm-specific AI systems, user-built agents and blank-slate workflow redesign. A small number of adjacent sources do not address the proposition directly, and one redirects attention toward long-term job and role creation; these variations do not overturn the period’s overall constructive development of the synthesis.

qs.q: And really, the key lever is how much agency the agent has, for lack of a better word, how  deterministic it is versus open-ended.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that agentic legal AI shifts from answer generation toward connected, tool-using work, while materially developing its practical implications. Common reasons include the value of orchestration, persistent matter context and fewer workflow handoffs, alongside the view that autonomy increases the importance of task-specific human intervention, verification, permissions and traceability. Concrete extensions include risk-tiered approval points, renewed vendor security reviews, unique agent identifiers, adversarial model review, expert acceptance and regression testing, permanent agent-management roles, client-specific tailoring and architectures integrating engagement, agency, work and context. Material variation concerns ambition and emphasis: some vendor and practitioner accounts predict end-to-end execution, self-service and substantial efficiencies; others stress that current tools are not like-for-like staff substitutes, that complex legal judgment remains outside reliable automation, and that verification may consume expensive lawyer time. Shaver and Black foreground governance gaps and propagated errors, whereas more optimistic sources emphasize workflow redesign and commercial opportunity. Arredondo redirects attention from agentic orchestration to reasoning models and verifiable rewards, while a small number of sources are too bounded or indirect to establish a clear position. Across the period, claimed capabilities and gains remain largely demonstrations, operational reports, forecasts and product descriptions rather than independent evidence of broad reliability or net savings.
